analysis.one_liner: Restricts union organizing by requiring bargaining units to be large groups of workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 33 Senate Republicans, never advanced past its referral to the Senate labor committee and died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that the National Labor Relations Board must treat bargaining units as large groups of workers who share many common interests, rather than the small groups of employees the Board approved in a 2011 decision and rulemaking. Under the bill, workers could be excluded from a unit only if their interests were truly distinct, and many factors — including the employer's organizational structure — would have to be weighed before an election. The practical effect is to make it harder for small groups of employees, such as a single department or a group of similar workers, to win union representation on their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers who face union organizing campaigns. By pushing the NLRB to define bargaining units broadly and to weigh factors like the employer's structure and workflow, the bill would make it harder for small groups of employees — a single department in a retail store, a wing of a nursing home, a group of similar workers in a larger plant — to form a union. It would also undo the Board's 2011 rules that sped up representation elections, giving employers more time to campaign against unions before a vote. Management-side law firms and employer trade associations that litigate and lobby on NLRB rules would also gain a more favorable statutory framework.

how_it_helps.text: Reverses the NLRB's August 2011 Specialty Healthcare decision, which allowed small 'micro-units' of workers to bargain, by requiring the Board to find a 'sufficient community of interest' among a broad group of employees before certifying a unit [S2][S3].
Also reverses the Board's June 2011 rulemaking speeding up union election procedures, restoring a slower election timeline in which employers have more time to campaign against representation [S2].

Requires the Board to weigh eight factors — including the employer's organizational structure and production process — before approving a unit, and prohibits excluding any group of employees unless its interests are sufficiently distinct, both of which push toward larger, harder-to-organize units [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers seeking to organize. Employees whose interests are shared with a larger, harder-to-organize workforce — for example, certified nursing assistants in one wing of a nursing home, or a department inside a large retailer — would lose the ability to win union representation as a small group. They would have to organize an entire broader unit or go without a union, and slower election rules would give employers more time to run counter-campaigns.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers trying to organize small units

drawbacks.text: The bill's core change would reverse a 2011 NLRB decision that let small, closely knit groups of employees bargain for themselves, meaning workers in fragmented workplaces could lose a path to representation they otherwise would have had [S2][S3].

The bill states its purpose as ensuring employees 'the fullest freedom in exercising the rights guaranteed by this Act' and argues that larger units avoid proliferation of fragmented bargaining units and match how businesses actually operate; supporters of the bill would say that is a fair reading of the law's intent, not an attack on workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to employers who gain a more favorable, predictable, and slower process for contested union elections. Its costs fall on a specific group of workers — those in small, cohesive units inside larger workforces — who would lose the ability to organize as a group under the standard the NLRB adopted in 2011. There is no compensating gain for working people in the bill's text; the arguments for it rest on the claim that larger units are more stable and better reflect employer structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened; the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Introduced on November 10, 2011, with 33 Republican cosponsors, and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S4][S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The bill expired at the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, the NLRB's 2011 Specialty Healthcare decision and its election-procedure rules were not reversed, so workers in small bargaining units kept the ability to organize that the bill would have taken away. Employers lost an opportunity to write that restriction into statute. Ultimately no one gained much: the bill simply stalled, leaving existing NLRB policy in place during a period when its legal footing was already being contested in the courts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Small-unit workers kept existing organizing rights

for.name: Johnny Isakson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1][S5].

for.name: 33 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill solid Republican support but no Democratic backing [S4].

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Tom Harkin, D-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; the bill's action history ends with the referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: All 33 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].

industries.industry: Employers facing union drives (retail, nursing homes, hospitality, franchise chains)
industries.note: The bill would have made it harder for small groups of their employees to unionize and given management more time to campaign before elections, directly reducing worker leverage [S2][S3].
Restricting micro-units and slowing elections shrinks the pool of workplaces unions can organize and the number of workers they can represent [S2][S3].
